title: The Personal Injury Lifecycle: Case Manager's Roadmap
summary: Master operational guide mapping the whole personal injury lifecycle for case managers: compliance, retainers and time logging, CMS and verification portals, liability systems, PIP/MedPay mechanics, property damage recovery, firm staff collaboration and the chronological file stages.
body:
### THE PERSONAL INJURY LIFECYCLE: CASE MANAGERS

### ROADMAP

*Master Operational Guide: Compliance, Tech Ecosystems, Liability Systems, and Asset Pipelines*

This master operational handout serves as an end-to-end framework mapping out Case Management Systems (CMS), verification portals, structural liability parameters, first-party coverage mechanics (PIP/MedPay), property damage recovery, core firm staff collaborations, and chronological file stages across the entire Personal Injury lifecycle. Use this as a foundational roadmap to be built upon in subsequent training manuals.

### Stage 1: Compliance Foundations, Retainers & Time Logging

- **The Contingency Fee Retainer:** Every file legally initializes here. Verify a signed, state-bar-compliant Retainer Agreement is executed in Casepeer upon onboarding. This contract establishes fee tiers and secures the Attorney Fee Lien against future settlement proceeds or verdicts.
- **HIPAA Compliance Mandate:** Protecting Protected Health Information (PHI) is a strict federal requirement under HIPAA. Secure an executed, date-specific HIPAA Release Form immediately during onboarding. Never disclose medical statuses or records to third parties without an audited release on file.
- **Billable Hours & Time Tracking:** Case Managers must log operational actions, telephone conferences, and file updates daily within Casepeer. Accurately tracking time ensures precise firm metric logging and preserves a clean record of case development activities.

### Stage 2: Tech Platforms, Request Portals & Staff Intersections

- **Casepeer CMS:** The central firm operating system used daily to log file notes, run time clocks, calendar medical deadlines, update provider treatment entries, and track staff pipelines.
- **Evidence Portals (Add123 & LexisNexis):** Verification channels used to pull asset searches, tag records, locate active driver policies, run background metrics, check municipal filings, and perform location trace queries.
- **Document Retrieval Portals (ChartSwap & Hippo):** Dedicated record retrieval engines utilized to request itemized clinic billing ledgers, secure radiology imaging, and request verified medical chart histories.

- **Federal Payor Gateways (CMS / BCRC Portal):** The mandatory gateway used to report injury files to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, track conditional payment letters, and monitor statutory Medicare super-lien totals.
- **Firm Staff Hierarchy & Collaboration:** Case Managers act as the central tactical anchor, coordinating workflows between the Intake Specialist (onboarding lead), Legal Assistant (administrative record requests support), Lien Specialist (lien reducer), Litigation Paralegal (court document support), Trial Attorney (legal advisor), and Accountant (trust accounting/disbursement gatekeeper).

### Stage 3: Investigative Intake, Multi-Party Action Plans & Coverage Hunting

- **Practice Area Intake Routing:** For Motor Vehicle Accidents (MVA), secure crash exchange files. For Premises Liability (Slip and Fall / Trip and Fall), secure corporate incident reports, surveillance footage preservation demands, and property maintenance logs. For Animal Liability (Dog Bites), identify the owner and request local Animal Control quarantine records.
- **Multi-Party Action Plans (Handling Passengers):** When an MVA involves multiple passengers in the client's vehicle, execute an immediate Passenger Conflict Audit. If the driver shares liability, the firm cannot represent both due to conflict of interest. If liability is 100% on the adverse vehicle, separate companion files are built to monitor treatment profiles simultaneously, ensuring an equitable pro-rata policy splitting model if limits are low.
- **Deep-Dive Insurance Identification:** Map all active insurance layers, including first-party (PIP/MedPay limits) and third-party BI caps. In low BI environments, query vehicle registration data via Add123 to unearth Separate Vehicle Owner Coverage (vicarious liability) or active underlying umbrella policies.
- **The Prior Injuries & History Audit:** Interview the client point-blank regarding historical medical and prior accident backgrounds. Discovering an unlogged pre-existing condition during a defense deposition can derail a case; identifying it at intake allows the firm to frame an objective 'structural aggravation of a baseline condition' from day one, neutralizing standard insurance defense strategies.

### Stage 4: Liability Assessment, Tort Elements & Fault Apportionment

- **The Legal Anatomy of Liability:** Case Managers must confirm the file satisfies the four distinct elements of negligence before submission: Duty of Care (obligations to act reasonably), Breach of Duty (failure to meet standards via action or omission), Causation (proximate link between breach and client trauma), and Damages (quantifiable medical/economic losses).
- **Fault Apportionment Systems:** Apply specific state jurisdictional risk models: (1) Pure Comparative Fault (recovery reduced by client's percentage of negligence), (2) Modified

Comparative Fault (recovery barred completely if negligence crosses a 50% or 51% bar threshold), and (3) Pure Contributory Negligence (any client fault of 1% or more completely bars recovery).

- **Liability Action Plans:** For MVAs, extract crash reports and dispatch logs. For Premises files, issue immediate certified Spoliation Letters demanding 2 hours of surveillance video surrounding the event and maintenance logs to prove Actual or Constructive Notice. For Dog Bites, extract history reports from Animal Control to verify strict liability or one-bite thresholds.

### Stage 5: Property Damage, Diminished Value & Loss of Use

- **The Operational Divide:** Handle vehicle damage files instantly to prevent administrative bottlenecks. Map third-party property damage limits early, and pivot to first-party Collision coverage if the adverse carrier stalls liability investigations, seeking deductible recovery via subrogation later.
- **Structural Valuation Auditing:** For repairable files, log hidden structural supplements from body shops in Casepeer. For Total Loss vehicles, review carrier appraisal reports (such as CCC ONE) line-by-line to ensure all options, tire conditions, and interior upgrades are perfectly accounted for in the Actual Cash Value (ACV).
- **Advanced Pockets of Value:** Pursue Loss of Use cash-out options based on local daily rental rates if the client does not require a physical rental vehicle. Audit clean-titled, late-model vehicles for Diminished Value claims by ordering certified history searches via Add123 to capture lost market equity post-repair.
- **Weaponizing Physical Impact:** Extract deep frame rails, floor pan buckling, and seat frame bending blueprints from shop supplements to combine into Section 1 of the BI Demand Packet, proving kinetic force transfer and reinforcing medical causation data.

### Stage 6: Calendar Management & Client Communication Frameworks

- **Proactive Calendar Management:** Enforce a strict zero-tolerance calendar policy. Every file must contain an active 'Next Action' task window in Casepeer to track statutory deadlines, records orders, and demand expirations. Never allow a file to sit dark without a task prompt.
- **The 30-Day Mandatory Client Contact Protocol:** Execute a mandatory voice-to-voice touchpoint with every active client at minimum every 30 days to log treatment updates, discover secondary clinical providers, and check ongoing wage impacts.
- **Treatment Mapping Coordination:** Logically map client care across sequential intervals: Acute Assessment (Days 1-14) -> Conservative Rehab Phase (Weeks 2-8) -> Advanced Diagnostics/MRIs (Weeks 4-6) -> Specialist Evaluations (Weeks 8+). Audit files bi-weekly to ensure treatment compliance and eliminate care gaps.

### Stage 7: No-Fault 'PIP Physics' & Medical Funding Coordination

- **The Emergency Medical Condition (EMC) Gatekeeper:** In statutory states, secure a signed clinical EMC declaration to unlock the full $10,000 policy. Files lacking an EMC are hard-capped at $2,500, causing insurance software evaluation engines to automatically tag the injury as a minor soft-tissue strain.
- **The Mandate to Exhaust PIP:** Ensure providers bill first-party PIP immediately to $0.00. This removes liability set-off reductions, validates diagnostic urgency to evaluation software, and shifts subsequent care into unmitigated, out-of-pocket special damages under a Letter of Protection (LOP), which acts as a direct multiplier on the general damages baseline.

### Stage 8: Medical Payments (MedPay) Coverage & First-Party Coordination

- **Contractual No-Fault Support:** MedPay acts as a no-fault contract layer separate from PIP. It carries no restrictive 14-day rule barriers and requires no active EMC signature to access funding limits ($1,000, $5,000, or $10,000 profiles). It universally steps in to pay for the remaining 20% clinical copay left behind by PIP to settle medical provider ledgers at 100% in real-time.
- **Strategic Funding Coordination:** Instruct clinics to establish a dual-billing template (80% to PIP and 20% to MedPay) to insulate the client from collections. If specialized surgical interventions or MRIs are pending, execute a MedPay Hold Letter to preserve liquid first-party cash pools, bypassing conservative billing tracks to fund advanced diagnostic facility fees directly.
- **Subrogation Risk Mitigation:** Unlike PIP, MedPay carriers maintain contractual reimbursement claims against third-party global settle pools. Case Managers must deploy the contractual Made-Whole Defense in low-limit scenarios to block reimbursement claims completely, or enforce a mandatory reduction cut based on our legal procurement fee percentage.

### Stage 9: Advanced Surgical & Interventional Injections Pipeline

- **Interventional Pain Procedures:** Track and categorize targeted injection types (Epidural Steroid Injections, Medial Branch Blocks, Radiofrequency Ablations) and secure matching operative logs. Operative notes must document objective pathology to register in adjuster databases.
- **Pre-Operative Case Management:** If surgery is recommended but pending, pull a formal signed surgical narrative from the specialist along with an itemized future cost projection to demand full policy limits based on future care models.
- **Post-Operative (Post-Op) Monitoring:** Coordinate post-op physical therapy schedules immediately to eliminate care caps. Ensure the surgeon documents permanent

anatomical hardware configurations, surgical scar dimensions, and permanent impairment ratings under the AMA Guides.

### Stage 10: Demand Architecture, Pre-Suit Affidavits & Attorney Deliberations

- **Algorithmic Valuation Optimization:** Configure demand packets to feed automated appraisal software (Colossus, ClaimIQ) explicit data targets: objective neurological deficits, CPT code line weights, and documented ADL disruptions.
- **Compulsory Document Inclusion Checklist:** Legal Assistant assembles demand components: (1) Certified CPT billing ledgers, (2) Corresponding provider clinical narratives, (3) Standalone raw radiologist report sheets for diagnostic imaging, and (4) Verified employer-signed lost wage forms. Case Manager audits for compliance before submission.
- **Pre-Suit Case Affidavit Matrix:** Deploy targeted legal disclosures before filing suit, including an Affidavit of No Additional Insurance from the defendant, an Affidavit of Sole Owner/Permissive Use, and a client Household Affidavit to anchor stacked coverage hooks.
- **UM/UIM Demand Pivot & Consent:** If BI limits are insufficient, pivot to UM tracks. Crucial Rule: You must request and secure a formal 'UM Waiver' or 'Consent to Settle' from the UM carrier before executing any third-party BI settlement release to preserve first-party rights.
- **Case Manager - Attorney Deliberations & Calibrations:** Before any demand packet is submitted or any final settlement posture is locked in, the Case Manager must execute a formal file deliberation and calibration session with the handling attorney. Use this review to run risk calculations, evaluate target value metrics, identify litigation exposure factors, and verify that all objective data points align perfectly with the core file strategy.

### Stage 11: Pre-Suit Settlements & Release Auditing

- **The Verbal Close & Confirmation:** Once a gross offer is accepted, dispatch an immediate confirmation email within 15 minutes to establish a binding paper trail and block insurer management rollbacks.
- **Release Agreement Auditing:** Review the insurance carrier’s formal Release document carefully. Ensure it is a 'Limited Release' or 'Proportionate Release' rather than a Global Release if a secondary UM or health insurance subrogation tracking is active, blocking global waiver language that could inadvertently kill secondary claims.
- **The Mandatory Sign-Off Protocol:** Never execute a liability release until the client has signed a comprehensive, line-by-line electronic disclosure sheet confirming they understand their bottom-line take-home net after fees, costs, and medical bill allocations.

### Stage 12: Formal Litigation, Mediation & Arbitration Pipelines

- **Filing & Written Discovery:** When pre-suit channels fail, the lawsuit is filed. Case Managers assist the Litigation Paralegal in compiling data for Requests for Production (RFPs) and Interrogatories. All provider bills and clinical notes must match previous disclosures perfectly to prevent defense exploitation.
- **Court-Ordered Mediation Standby:** Parties meet before a certified neutral mediator. Case Managers remain on standby during mediation to execute real-time phone conferences with clinical providers to secure conditional reduction caps if a global settlement number becomes attainable.
- **Binding Arbitration Awards:** In select instances, the case enters private binding arbitration. The private arbiter or panel issues a final Binding Arbitration Award that dictates the absolute closing payout of the file, carrying no avenue for judicial appeal.

### Stage 13: Subrogation, Settlement Liens & Statutory Reductions

- **ERISA Self-Funded Plans:** Employer plans backed by federal ERISA mandates hold strict first-priority recovery rights. Demand Plan Documents (Summary Plan Description and Form 5500) to confirm status, then negotiate a voluntary procurement-cost reduction based on firm fees.
- **Private Health Insurance:** Governed by state insurance statutes. Leverage the contractual Made-Whole Doctrine to secure full subrogation waivers if policy limits failed to compensate the client completely.
- **Medicare Super-Liens:** Federal Secondary Payer statutory mandate. Manage payments early via the BCRC portal. Medicare holds a federal super-lien taking priority over all other parties and automatically applies an administrative reduction for procurement fees upon final closing.
- **Medicaid State Claims:** Medicaid recovery is strictly hard-capped by U.S. Supreme Court precedent (Ahlborn/Gallardo) at the specific portion of the settlement explicitly allocated for past medical expenses caps, protecting pain and suffering awards from balance sweeps.
- **Pro-Rata Provider Reductions:** For standard medical clinic liens and LOP balances, enforce the Pro-Rata Mandate using a formal Proportional Reduction Proposal to resolve clinic lien deadlocks equitably based on available fund caps.

### Stage 14: Disbursement, Trust Accounting & File Closure

- **Settlement Distribution Sheet (SDS):** Draft the line-item financial distribution ledger, matching penny-for-penny: Gross Settlement − Attorney Fees − Firm Costs − Negotiated Medical Liens/Subrogation = Client Net Recovery. This calculation satisfies the underlying Attorney Lien and matches the closing ledger boundaries.

- **IOLTA Account Reconciliation:** Verify that the carrier check has been deposited into the firm's Interest on Lawyers' Trust Accounts (IOLTA) and completely cleared by the bank. Never disburse funds on an uncleared instrument.
- **Closing Execution & Lien Waivers:** Upon client signature of the SDS, process firm fee transfers and medical payor distributions. Case Managers must secure a signed, final, notarized Lien Waiver and Release form from every medical provider to shield the client and firm from future collection efforts.

### Stage 15: Operational Evidentiary Compliance & Cost Matrix

#### Case Hardening Cost Category (Add123 & Postal Channels):

| Query Type / Verification Channel | Firm Cost Rate |
|---|---|
| Comprehensive Driver's License History Query (Add123) | $3.42 |
| Certified VIN / Asset Title History Search (Add123) | $3.42 |
| Municipal Tag and License Plate Registration Search (Add123) | $1.74 |
| Real-Time Civil Insurance Coverage Verification Query (Add123) | $3.00 |

**Outbound Document Scale:** Regular First Class Mail is billed at $0.69; Secure Summons Package Priority Delivery is $8.50; Certified Mail with Return Receipt Requested (Formal Tenders) is $8.69; Priority Mail with Signature Confirmation (Litigation Invoices) is $12.20.

### Case Managers Master Lifecycle Checklist

☐Compliance Foundations: Verify a signed Contingency Fee Retainer, fully audited HIPAA release, and primary billable hours entries are logged in Casepeer.

☐SOL Verification: Confirm the correct Date of Loss is logged in our system and checked against statutory parameters.

☐Proactive Calendar Tasks: Confirm every file contains an active 'Next Action' task window with zero unassigned gaps.

☐Client Contact Tracking: Verify a voice-to-voice communication event has been executed and logged within the last 30 days.

☐Multi-Party Passenger Audit: Verify separate companion files are built and conflict checks cleared for passenger action plans.

☐ Liability Anatomy Verification: Confirm file evidence establishes Duty, Breach, Causation, and Damages relative to jurisdictional fault rules.

☐Property Damage Supplement Check: Ensure deep structural impact photos and mechanical supplements are indexed to prove kinetic force transfer.

☐MedPay Allocation Check: Verify if an 80/20 split or a formal MedPay Hold is structurally required to fund specialized facility care lines.

☐ Demand Document Inclusions: Verify certified billing ledgers, corresponding narratives, raw radiologist reports, and employer wage verifications are compiled before packet shipment.

☐Attorney Calibration Check: Confirm a formal file review and calibration session has been executed with the attorney prior to demand delivery.

☐Advanced Procedures Tracking: Ensure injection operative logs, surgical narratives, pre-op cost models, and post-op therapy notes are indexed within the architecture.

☐Affidavit Verification Check: Ensure the proper Affidavit of No Additional Insurance or Household Affidavit is executed to secure hidden policy layers.

☐Lien & Statutory Subrogation Audit: Identify health payor parameters (ERISA, Medicare, Medicaid, Private) and order updated audit ledgers to eliminate unrelated charges.

☐Lien Control & Waivers Map: Confirm clinic liens are mapped and that final provider release and waiver receipts are signed and stored.

☐IOLTA Reconciliation: Ensure the settlement funds have completely cleared the firm's trust account prior to printing disbursement checks.

title: Handling Treatment Gaps in the Demand Phase
summary: How treatment gaps hurt the value and credibility of a personal injury case, what adjusters argue because of them, and the possible outcomes of leaving a gap unaddressed, such as reduced offers and denied medical bills.
body:
## Handling Treatment Gaps in the Demand Phase

#### Impact of Treatment Gaps

Treatment gaps can significantly affect the value and credibility of a personal injury case because insurance adjusters may argue that:

- The injuries were minor or resolved
- The client was not truly in pain
- Treatment was unnecessary or excessive
- Another event caused the current symptoms
- The client failed to mitigate damages

#### Even short unexplained gaps can weaken settlement leverage and are a common reason for claim denial.

## Possible Outcomes of Unaddressed Gaps

#### Reduced Settlement Offers

Adjusters may lower the value of:

- Pain and suffering
- Future treatment claims
- Permanency allegations

#### Denial of Certain Medical Bills

Insurers may refuse to pay for treatment occurring after the gap.

#### Increased Litigation Risk

Large or repeated gaps may cause:

- More aggressive defense challenges
- Requests for IMEs (Independent Medical Exams)
- Higher chance of disputed causation

#### Credibility Issues

Inconsistent treatment timelines can create concerns regarding:

- Symptom severity
- Client reliability
- Medical necessity

## Proactive Case Management: Preventing Gaps

Maintaining accurate treatment timelines is essential to clearly link medical care to the accident, strengthen the claim, and provide reliable documentation for negotiations or trial.

#### 1. Create a Clear Medical Chronology

The medical chronology serves as the foundation for the medical summary and allows for the entire medical journey to be seen in order.

- Review appointment timelines, provider records, billing dates, and referral delays.
- The chronology is the primary tool to easily detect gaps or inconsistencies in the records.

#### 2. Coordinate Treatment and Support

The treating phase is often the longest part of a personal injury case, requiring careful tracking.

- Coordinate care across multiple providers to prevent conflicting treatments and ensure consistent recovery.
- Track and monitor clients’ treatments and appointments to maintain case credibility, as delays in seeking treatment significantly weaken the case.
- Medical liens can be used to allow clients to continue treatment without out-of-pocket payments while awaiting a settlement.

#### Careful tracking of medical treatment and bills is essential because insurance negotiations depend on complete and accurate records.

## Strategies for Handling Existing Treatment Gaps

#### 1. Obtain and Document a Valid Reason

Document valid explanations for any interruption, as a documented explanation is better than silence:

- Financial hardship
- Transportation limitations
- Work schedule conflicts or inability to miss additional workdays
- Insurance authorization delays or denials
- Delayed specialist referrals
- Temporary symptom improvement

- Family emergencies

#### 2. Support the Explanation with Comprehensive Evidence

Whenever possible, include specific documentation to back up the explanation:

- **Medical Evidence:** Provider notes (SOAP notes), Emergency Medical Services (EMS) reports, Hospital/Emergency room reports, Imaging (MRI, X-ray), and specialist evaluations.
- **Scheduling/Admin Records:** Scheduling records, referral delay communications, insurance denials or authorization issues.
- **Client Records:** Client statements, employment conflicts, or documentation of financial hardship.

#### 3. Show Continuity of Symptoms

The goal is to show the injury never truly resolved and that complaints remained consistent before and after the gap.

- Emphasize recurring complaints before and after the interruption.
- Highlight continued pain or functional limitations.
- Reference objective findings (MRI, imaging, specialist evaluations) to reinforce the injury’s severity.

## Addressing the Gap Directly in the Demand Package

One of the biggest mistakes is pretending the treatment gap does not exist. A direct and well-supported explanation helps control the narrative before the adjuster uses the gap against the claim.

#### 1. Acknowledge the Gap Clearly

Do not hide or avoid discussing the interruption. Transparency strengthens credibility.

- Identify the specific time period of the gap (e.g., “temporary interruption between March 2 and April 10, 2026”).
- State that treatment was interrupted and address it professionally and factually.

#### 2. Explain the Circumstances Behind the Gap

Provide context to humanize the interruption and show it was reasonable under the circumstances.

*Example:* “The interruption resulted from delayed authorization for specialty care and the client’s inability to miss additional workdays during that period.”

#### 3. Reconnect the Treatment Timeline

Show that the client resumed treatment, and the care progression continued appropriately, preventing the adjuster from arguing the injury was resolved.

- Show that symptoms continued and complaints remained consistent.
- Use follow-up provider notes, continued pain complaints, MRI/imaging findings, and physical therapy progress reports as evidence. *Example:* “Upon resuming care, the client continued reporting neck pain, headaches, and reduced range of motion consistent with prior documented complaints.”

#### 4. Reinforce Medical Necessity

Tie the resumed treatment back to the accident-related injuries and ongoing objective findings.

- This helps defend all medical bills, future care recommendations, and pain and suffering claims. *Example:* “The continued course of treatment remained medically necessary due to persistent cervical complaints supported by MRI findings and physician evaluations.”

## Strategic Goal in the Demand Package

A strong demand package does not aim for a “perfect” case. Instead, it:

- Anticipates defense arguments
- Addresses weaknesses proactively
- Preserves credibility
- Reduces adjuster leverage
- Protects overall settlement value

#### A transparent and detailed explanation often carries more weight than attempting to avoid the issue entirely.

title: Insurance Coverage in Personal Injury Claims: What Applies, Who Pays and How to Find It
summary: A complete guide for case managers: the insurance coverages in an injury claim (liability, UM/UIM, MedPay, PIP, umbrella, commercial, rideshare, health and workers' compensation), how they fit together, how to find every policy, how to read a declarations page, and common coverage problems.
body:
*A guide for case managers and claims staff. Insurance rules, minimum limits and deadlines differ by state and by policy. Use this as a framework, read the actual policy, and confirm anything unclear with the handling attorney.*

## 1. Why coverage comes first

In a personal injury claim, the money for the client usually comes from insurance, not from the at-fault person's pocket. A strong case with no coverage behind it can be worth far less than an average case with a large policy. That is why coverage is checked at intake, again when a claim is opened, and again before demanding or settling.

Three questions drive everything:

1. **Who is responsible?** (liability: who was at fault, and who else may share responsibility)
2. **What insurance applies?** (every policy that could pay: theirs, ours, the employer's, an umbrella)
3. **How much is available, and in what order?** (limits, deductibles, offsets and who pays first)

## 2. Insurance basics every case manager should know

| Term | What it means in a claim |
|---|---|
| **Insurer (carrier)** | The company that issued the policy and will pay or deny the claim. |
| **Policyholder / named insured** | The person or business who bought the policy. |
| **Insured** | Anyone the policy covers: the named insured, resident family members, and often other people who drive the car with permission (permissive users). |
| **Policy period** | The dates the policy was in force. The accident date must fall inside it. |
| **Premium** | The price paid for the policy. A lapse for non-payment can end coverage. |
| **Limits** | The most the insurer will pay for a covered claim. |
| **Deductible** | The part the insured pays before the policy pays. It mostly applies to first-party property coverage such as collision. |
| **Endorsement (rider)** | A change added to the policy that adds, removes or changes coverage. |
| **Exclusion** | A situation the policy does not cover, such as using a personal car for delivery work or an excluded driver. |
| **Declarations page (dec page)** | The summary page of the policy: insured names, vehicles, coverage types, limits, deductibles and policy dates. It is the first document to ask for. |
| **Claim number / policy number** | The numbers to put on every letter, call and email to the carrier. |

### First-party and third-party claims (1P and 3P)

- **First-party (1P):** a claim against *our own client's* insurance company, such as PIP, MedPay, UM/UIM or collision. The client has a contract with that insurer. Coverage and limits are usually easy to confirm and the adjuster will confirm them quickly.
- **Third-party (3P):** a claim against *the at-fault person's* insurance company, such as bodily injury (BI) liability and property damage (PD). The client has no contract with that insurer. The adjuster often does not confirm coverage right away, asks for more information first and runs their own investigation.

Knowing which kind of claim you are opening tells you who to contact, what to expect and what to ask for.

## 3. The coverages you will see in injury cases

### 3.1 Liability coverage (pays for harm the insured causes to others)

- **Bodily injury (BI) liability** pays for injuries the insured causes to other people: medical bills, lost income, pain and suffering. It also pays the insured's legal defense if they are sued. This is the main coverage in most third-party injury claims.
- **Property damage (PD) liability** pays for damage the insured causes to other people's property, mainly vehicles.

**How limits are written.**
- *Split limits*, for example **25/50/25** (written $25,000 / $50,000 / $25,000): $25,000 per person for bodily injury, $50,000 total per accident for bodily injury, and $25,000 for property damage.
- *Combined single limit (CSL)*, for example **$100,000 CSL**: one total amount for all injury and property damage from one accident, however it is divided.

State minimums are often low. For example, Nevada's minimum is 25/50/20 (confirm the current figure for the state of the accident). Many at-fault drivers carry only the minimum, which is often less than the injuries are worth. That is why the other coverages below matter.

### 3.2 Uninsured and underinsured motorist coverage (UM/UIM)

- **Uninsured motorist (UM)** protects our client's own policy when the at-fault driver has *no* insurance, or flees the scene (hit and run).
- **Underinsured motorist (UIM)** applies when the at-fault driver has insurance, but *not enough* to cover the client's damages.

UM/UIM is bought on the client's *own* policy (and sometimes can be used under a household member's policy), so it is a first-party claim. Points to check:

- **Limits and "stacking".** Some states allow combining UM/UIM limits from several vehicles or policies. Others do not.
- **Offset or add-on.** In some states UIM pays only the difference between the damages and the at-fault driver's limits, up to the UIM limit. In others it is added on top of the at-fault driver's payment. The policy and state law decide.
- **Notice and consent.** Many policies require notifying the UIM insurer *before* accepting the at-fault driver's limits, and getting its consent or waiver, so the UIM claim is not lost. Missing this step can forfeit the coverage. Ask the attorney before any limits settlement.
- **Hit and run.** Many states require a prompt police report, and sometimes physical contact with the other vehicle, to make a UM claim.
- **Time limits.** UM/UIM claims can have their own contract deadlines, sometimes shorter than the statute of limitations. Calendar them.

### 3.3 Medical payments coverage (MedPay)

Optional coverage on the client's own auto policy that pays medical bills for the insured and passengers *regardless of fault*, up to a limit (often $1,000 to $10,000). It usually pays quickly, can cover deductibles and co-pays, and often does not require proof of fault. Check whether the policy lets the insurer be repaid from the settlement (reimbursement) or not.

### 3.4 Personal injury protection (PIP) and no-fault

In *no-fault* states, the client's own PIP coverage pays medical bills and often part of lost income first, whoever caused the crash. A claim against the at-fault driver is allowed only after a threshold is met (a dollar amount of medical bills, or a type of serious injury, depending on the state). In other states, PIP is optional and works much like MedPay but with broader benefits. PIP is a first-party claim, so the adjuster confirms coverage quickly.

### 3.5 Property coverages

- **Collision** pays to repair or replace the client's own vehicle after a crash, whoever is at fault, less the deductible. It is mandatory if the car is financed or leased.
- **Comprehensive** pays for non-crash damage such as theft, vandalism, weather, fire or hitting an animal.
- **Rental / loss of use** pays for a substitute vehicle while the car is repaired. If the other driver is at fault, loss of use can be claimed from their insurer.
- **Total loss and diminished value.** If repair costs exceed a set share of the car's value, the car is a total loss and the insurer pays its value. A repaired car can still lose market value (diminished value), which can be claimed from the at-fault party's insurer in many states.

### 3.6 Umbrella and excess coverage

An **umbrella** or **excess** policy adds liability coverage on top of the underlying auto or home policy, often $1 million or more. It applies only after the primary limits are paid. It is easy to miss, so always ask whether the at-fault person or business has one.

### 3.7 Coverage tied to business and work

- **Commercial auto and business policies.** If the at-fault driver was working (delivering, driving a company vehicle, or driving a truck), the employer's policy may apply, often with much higher limits. Federal law sets higher minimum limits for many trucks. The employer can also be responsible for the employee's negligence (vicarious liability, or *respondeat superior*).
- **Hired and non-owned auto coverage.** Covers a business when its employees drive their own or rented cars for work.
- **Workers' compensation.** If the client was hurt while working, workers' compensation pays medical bills and part of lost wages whoever caused the crash, but it generally prevents suing the employer. A separate claim against a *third party* who caused the injury may still be possible, and the workers' compensation insurer will have a lien on it.
- **Rideshare (Uber, Lyft and similar).** Coverage depends on the driver's app status: *app off* (the driver's personal policy), *app on and waiting for a ride* (a lower company policy), and *accepted a ride or carrying a passenger* (typically much higher company liability coverage, often $1 million). The status at the moment of the crash must be documented.

### 3.8 Property and premises coverage

- **Homeowners and renters policies** include liability coverage for injuries on the property and, often, *medical payments to others* without proving fault.
- **Commercial general liability (CGL)** covers businesses for customer and visitor injuries (slip and fall, for example).
- **Landlord, property manager and contractor policies** may also apply. Ask who owned, leased, maintained and controlled the property.

### 3.9 The client's health insurance and other benefits

These are *not* sources of recovery from the at-fault party, but they affect the case because they pay bills, and often have repayment rights from the settlement:

- **Private health insurance and ERISA plans.** May claim reimbursement. Self-funded ERISA plans can have strong rights, subject to the plan terms.
- **Medicare and Medicaid.** Have legal rights to be repaid for accident-related care (conditional payments and Medicaid liens). Report them early.
- **Short- and long-term disability insurance.** May pay lost income and may have repayment rights.
- **Provider liens and letters of protection (LOP).** Providers who treat on a promise of payment from the settlement.

## 4. Who pays first? How the coverages fit together

Coverages are usually used in a sensible order. The exact order depends on the state and the policies, but a common pattern for a car crash is:

1. **MedPay or PIP** (the client's own policy) pays early medical bills, regardless of fault.
2. **The client's health insurance** may pay bills that MedPay/PIP does not cover (and will want repayment).
3. **The at-fault driver's BI liability** is the main source for the injury claim, up to its limits.
4. **UIM** (client's own policy) pays the gap if the at-fault limits are not enough.
5. **Umbrella/excess** or **an employer's policy** adds more if available.
6. **Property:** the at-fault driver's PD liability pays for the car, or the client uses collision and the insurer later seeks repayment.

### A worked example

A client's medical bills and other damages are valued at $120,000. The at-fault driver carries 25/50/25. The client has MedPay of $5,000 and UIM of $100,000/$300,000.

| Source | Amount | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| MedPay (client's policy) | $5,000 | Paid early; check for any reimbursement right. |
| At-fault BI liability | $25,000 | The per-person limit is the most this policy pays. |
| UIM (client's policy) | Up to the gap | Pays the difference between the damages and the at-fault limits, up to $100,000, under an offset-type policy. Prior notice and consent were needed before taking the $25,000. |
| Remaining shortfall | Depends | If damages still exceed everything, ask whether an umbrella, an employer policy or other coverage exists. |

The point of the example is the *process*: find every coverage, check the limits and the rules of each, and sequence the claims so no coverage is lost.

## 5. The coverage hunt: how to find every policy

Work through this checklist and document each answer in the case management system.

**At intake, ask the client:**
- Who owned and who drove each vehicle in the crash? Was anyone working or driving for an app?
- What auto insurance does the client have? Collision? MedPay or PIP? UM/UIM? What limits?
- Does anyone in the household have a separate auto policy? Any umbrella policy?
- What health insurance, Medicare, Medicaid or disability coverage does the client have?
- Was the client at work or on a work errand?

**About the at-fault side:**
- The at-fault driver's insurer, policy number and claim number (from the crash report or exchange of information).
- The *owner* of the at-fault vehicle, if different from the driver. Their policy may also apply.
- The driver's employer and whether the driver was working.
- Other possible defendants: a property owner, a business, a vehicle owner, a government body.

**How to confirm coverage:**
- Send the **letter of representation (LOR)** to every insurer. Ask the adjuster to confirm coverage, policy limits and any other insurance, and to send the declarations page. Some states require insurers to disclose limits on request, and others do not.
- Ask the at-fault party's lawyer or insurer for any **umbrella or excess** policy.
- Get the confirmation **in writing**. A verbal answer is not enough.
- In a lawsuit, **discovery** allows requests for all insurance policies that may cover the claim, and the federal rules require disclosure of insurance agreements.
- Note **reservation of rights letters** (the insurer pays under conditions) and **denials**, and send them to the attorney right away.

## 6. Reading a declarations page: a quick checklist

- Are the **named insured** and the **driver/vehicle** correct?
- Is the **accident date** inside the **policy period**?
- Is the **vehicle listed** (or covered as a replacement or a newly acquired vehicle)?
- Which **coverages** are shown, and what are the **limits** for each?
- Are there **endorsements** that add or remove coverage?
- Are there **excluded drivers** or business-use limits?
- Is the policy **personal or commercial**?

If the dec page and the facts do not match (wrong driver, unlisted vehicle, lapsed policy), tell the attorney. These are the situations where coverage is disputed.

## 7. Common coverage problems and how to respond

| Problem | What it means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| **No insurance / lapsed policy** | The at-fault driver had no coverage on the date. | Check the client's UM coverage, other responsible parties (owner, employer) and the attorney's advice on collecting from the person. |
| **Low limits** | The at-fault policy is far below the damages. | Look for UIM, umbrella, employer or owner coverage. Follow the notice and consent rules before accepting limits. |
| **Reservation of rights** | The insurer is investigating whether it must cover the claim. | Alert the attorney. Keep records of every notice and date. |
| **Coverage denial** | The insurer says the claim is not covered (excluded driver, intentional act, business use). | Get the denial in writing. The attorney decides whether to challenge it. |
| **Late notice** | A policy requires prompt notice and it was not given. | Give notice immediately to every possibly responsible insurer, and document it. |
| **Permissive use** | The driver was not the owner. Coverage for permissive users depends on the policy and state. | Identify the owner's policy and any policy on the driver. |
| **Shared fault / multiple defendants** | Several people may share responsibility. | Open claims against each, and track every policy and limit. |
| **Government vehicle** | Different notice rules, short deadlines and caps may apply. | Calendar the notice-of-claim deadline immediately and tell the attorney. |
| **Unreasonable refusal to pay** | The insurer delays or refuses a clearly valid claim. | Document everything. The attorney decides on a bad faith claim. |

## 8. How coverage shapes the rest of the case

- **Demand strategy:** the demand is aimed at the limits that exist. If the injuries clearly exceed the limits, the attorney may send a **policy limits demand**, sometimes with a deadline. This needs the attorney's decision.
- **Releases:** a release with the at-fault insurer can end the case against that person. Read it with the attorney, and keep the UIM rights intact.
- **Liens and net recovery:** repayment rights of health plans, Medicare, Medicaid, providers and MedPay/PIP carriers reduce what the client keeps. Identify them early. They are the reason coverage and liens are always handled together.
- **Tracking:** record each insurer, adjuster, claim number, limits, coverage confirmation date, notices sent and deadlines, in one place in the case file.

## 9. Common mistakes to avoid

- Waiting for the other side to volunteer coverage information.
- Accepting a limits settlement before UIM notice and consent are handled.
- Forgetting an umbrella policy, an owner's policy or an employer's policy.
- Not opening the client's own MedPay or PIP claim early.
- Missing a short UM/UIM or notice-of-claim deadline.
- Relying on a verbal confirmation of limits.
- Treating a reservation of rights letter as routine.
- Overlooking rideshare status, workers' compensation or Medicare involvement.

## 10. Quick reference: coverage types

| Coverage | Whose policy | Pays for | Fault needed? |
|---|---|---|---|
| BI liability | At-fault party | Injuries to other people | Yes |
| PD liability | At-fault party | Damage to other people's property | Yes |
| UM / UIM | Client's | Injuries when the at-fault party has no or too little insurance | Yes (the other party's) |
| MedPay | Client's | Medical bills | No |
| PIP | Client's | Medical bills and some lost income | No |
| Collision | Client's | Client's own vehicle repair or replacement | No |
| Comprehensive | Client's | Theft, weather, vandalism, animals | No |
| Umbrella / excess | At-fault party's | Liability above the primary limits | Yes |
| Commercial / employer | Employer's | Injuries caused by an employee at work | Yes |
| Homeowners / CGL | Property owner's | Injuries on the property | Usually |
| Workers' compensation | Employer's | Work injuries | No |

## 11. Terms to know

All of these are in the Glossary: **Policy Limits, Declarations Page, Bodily Injury (BI), Property Damage (PD), First-Party Claim, Third-Party Claim, UM / UIM, PIP, MedPay, No-Fault, Excess / Umbrella Policy, Deductible, Premium, Letter of Representation (LOR), Letter of Protection (LOP), Total Loss, Diminished Value, Loss of Use, Subrogation, Medicare Conditional Payment, ERISA Plan, Made-Whole Doctrine, Bad Faith, Policy Limits Demand, Vicarious Liability, Workers' Compensation.**
